title: Remount
teaches: The remount as we trade it: a leader loses a line for real, an average or a price level it held, then retakes it with a clear green close. We buy after a quiet day holds above the line, with a market order over that day's high and a real stop a few cents under its low. The close must be above the 200-day, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and most tries lose small.

August 7 it trades over that high. Buy at market, 101.19. Stop 99.98, under the inside day's low. 1.2% away.
The stop is the exit, not a close under the line. 3R came the next day. It ran to 25.0R.

walkthroughs.title: AMD, November 2023: the reaction day remount
steps: AMD reported October 31, 2023, after the close. Next day, November 1, it took back the 50-day on the gap.
We don't buy the 3 days before a report. This is after, so it counts.
Quiet day's high is 109.41. November 3 it trades over: buy at market, 109.42. Stop 105.86, under the quiet day's low.
That's 3.3%, wider than I like. So fewer shares, never a tighter stop. It ran to 21.2R.

walkthroughs.title: DOCU, March 2024: a planned loss
steps: DOCU spent a long stretch under its 50-day. March 11, 2024, it remounts. Then a quiet inside day above the line.
March 14 it clears the quiet day's high. Buy at market, 59.54. Stop 58.44, under its low, 1.8% away.
It falls straight through the stop, and the trade's done. The stop is the exit.
Then it held the 50-day for 20 sessions and reached 61.47. Right level. That trigger just didn't run.

questions.q: A leader sat under its 50-day for three weeks. Today it closes back over it on a clear green candle. What are you looking at?
choices: A breakout from a flat base
questions.why: That's a Remount. The stock didn't just tag the 50-day. It lost it, lived under it for three weeks, and now it's taken it back on a clear close. That's the whole idea: a line lost for real, then retaken. A dip of a day or two that snaps right back never really lost the line. We'd call that a pullback or a U&R, and you trade it differently.
questions.lesson_line: Lost for real, then taken back. That's a Remount.

wrong.An Oops, a one-day reversal: An Oops happens inside one session, off the prior day's low. This stock spent three weeks under the line.
wrong.A breakout from a flat base: A breakout clears a ceiling from below. This one took back a line it had lost.
wrong.A bounce off a rising 50-day: A bounce means the line held. Here it broke, and the stock lived under it for weeks.

questions.simple: It lost the 50-day for real, then took it back on a clear close. That's a Remount.

reasons: +2 what 'lost for real' means rests on a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A Remount's line can be the 50-day or 200-day, or a flat price level the stock held before it broke.
questions.why: True. Two kinds of line, one setup. The average kind is the 50-day or the 200-day. The level kind is a price that acted as a floor. Think an old pivot, a base low, an old high or a round number. Either way you're trading the same thing. The stock loses the line for real, takes it back on a clear close, and you buy over the quiet day after.
questions.lesson_line: An average or a level. Same trade either way.
questions.simple: True. The line can be a big average, or a price level that held as a floor before it broke.

questions.q: For the moving-average kind of Remount, which lines are you watching the stock lose and take back?
questions.why: The 50-day and the 200-day. Those are the lines everybody watches. When a leader loses one for a while and takes it back, a lot of people see it. That's what gives the retake weight. The 9 and 20 EMA are our trail lines. We use them to sell what's left of a winner, not to call a Remount.
questions.lesson_line: 50-day or 200-day. The 9 and 20 are for selling.

wrong.The 5-day and the 8-day: Those are short lines a stock crosses all the time. Losing one means nothing.
wrong.The 100-day and the 150-day: We don't run those. Our charts carry the 9 and 20 EMA with the 50 and 200 SMA.
wrong.The 9 and 20 EMA: Those are our trail lines. We sell what's left on a close below them.

questions.simple: The 50-day and the 200-day. The short EMAs are for trailing a winner, not for this setup.

reasons: +2 which lines count rests on a held decision (D-073)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A stock's still under its 50-day but ripping toward it midday. Buying now, before the close, is the smart Remount entry.
questions.why: False. No close over the line, no Remount. A stock ripping toward the line at noon can still close right under it. Buy it then and you own a failed try. There's no quiet day yet either, so there's no low to put your stop under. Wait for the close over the line, then the quiet day, then buy over its high. A better price isn't better if the trade never set up.
questions.lesson_line: No close over the line, no Remount. Don't jump the gun.
questions.simple: False. It isn't a Remount until it closes over the line, so buying early can leave you in a failed try.

deeper.trap: StockCharts says the same about any moving average cross: wait for a full candle close above it. Buying a poke a few cents over the line is the same mistake.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We never buy a Remount with the close below the ___-day SMA.
questions.why: 200. We never buy a Remount with the close below the 200-day SMA. A 200-day remount is the cross itself.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, every time.
questions.simple: The close must be above the 200-day average, and we do not buy a Remount below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook (no longs below the 200-day)

questions.q: The quiet day's high is 50.00. A limit order to buy at 50.00 is how you get into this Remount.
questions.why: False. We buy with a market order as price trades through 50.00. A limit order can't do that job. Rest it there while price is under 50.00 and it fills right away, before the break. Put it in after the break and a fast move leaves it behind. That fast move is the one you wanted. Your stop's a real order too, a few cents under the quiet day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Market order in on the break. Real stop order under the low.
questions.simple: False. You buy at market as it trades over the high, since a limit fills too early or gets left behind.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, D41)

questions.q: When a leader takes back a lost 50-day and holds it, the line that was a ceiling can become a floor again.
questions.why: True. While a stock lives under a lost 50-day, that line works as a ceiling. Funds that got stuck use it as a place to sell. A clean retake gets through that selling, and the line can go back to being support. That's the edge in the setup. It's an idea, not a promise. The line can get lost again, and that's what your stop is for.
questions.lesson_line: A lost line is a ceiling. Take it back and it's a floor.
questions.simple: True. A lost line acts like a ceiling, and a clean retake can make it a floor again.

deeper.example: IBD's take: once a stock is under its 50-day, institutions may use the line to mark a sell level. It often takes a big boost of buying to muscle back above it.

questions.q: A 50-day Remount only counts if the close is over the 200-day too.
questions.why: True. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard no, with no exception for a stock. So a stock can retake its 50-day all it wants. If the close is still under the 200-day, the bigger trend is down and you'd be buying a bounce in a downtrend. Check the 200-day first, then the 50.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day first. Under it, it's not a buy.
questions.simple: True. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, so the close has to clear it too.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)

deeper.counter: StockCharts says the same thing: look for bullish crosses only when price is already above the longer average, the 200-day.

questions.q: A big leader closes under its 50-day and stays under. Per IBD, what may the funds do with that line now?
choices: Use it as a place to sell
Treat it as a floor to buy
Add to their longs near it
questions.answer: Use it as a place to sell
questions.why: Use it as a place to sell. That's IBD's read: once a stock is under its 50-day, institutions may use the line to mark a sell level. Think about why. A fund that held through the break wants out on a bounce back to it. That's why a real Remount needs real buying to get back over. A weak drift up into the line often just feeds those sellers.
questions.lesson_line: A lost 50-day is where stuck funds sell. Getting back over takes real buying.

wrong.Treat it as a floor to buy: That was the deal before it broke. Once it's lost, IBD says funds may sell there.
wrong.Ignore it, watch the 200-day: IBD's point is about the 50-day itself. Big holders watch it closely.
wrong.Add to their longs near it: IBD says the opposite. The lost line marks where they may sell.

questions.simple: Funds stuck under a lost 50-day may sell into it. That's why taking it back needs real buying.

reasons: the key rests on one cited IBD quote (i2)

questions.q: A Remount counts once price pokes a few cents over the line during the day.
questions.why: False. A remount needs a full candle close above the line. ChartSchool says to wait for a full candle close above the average before calling a cross. A marginal poke a few cents over the line during the day is not a remount day, and buying it is a listed mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Close it above. A poke is not a retake.
questions.simple: False. A retake counts only when the day closes above the line, not when price touches it for a moment.

questions.q: IBD reads a weak, low-volume rise after a high-volume drop under the 50-day as what?
questions.why: A chance to sell. IBD says a high-volume decline to or below the 50-day, followed by a weak low-volume rise, is your chance to sell. A stock often needs a large boost of buying power to muscle back above a lost 50-day line. A light rise does not show it. So it is not a Remount to buy, and our card lists buying that drift as a mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A light drift back after a heavy drop is a sell, not a buy.

wrong.A Remount to buy: IBD says the opposite. A light rise after a heavy drop is a sell, and our card lists it as a mistake.
wrong.A reason to add: A weak rise gives no reason to add.
wrong.A confirmed bottom: A weak, low-volume rise confirms nothing.

questions.simple: IBD reads it as a chance to sell, because a weak rise on low volume lacks the buying power to retake the line.

reasons: the light-volume invalidation is proposed on card 13 and held (D-006)

questions.q: A stock reports after the close and takes back its 50-day the next day on the reaction. That remount can be a buy.
questions.why: True. We don't take new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report can gap a stock right through your stop. On the reaction day the report's already out, so that risk is gone. AMD did this: it reported after the close on 2023-10-31 and took back its 50-day on the reaction day. You still wait for the quiet day and buy over its high.
questions.lesson_line: After the report is fair game. Before it isn't.
questions.simple: True. The report is already out, so the ban on buying just before a report doesn't apply.

deeper.example: AMD reported after the close on 2023-10-31 and closed back over its 50-day on 2023-11-01. The quiet day's high was 109.41. The buy came on 2023-11-03 at 109.42 with the stop at 105.86, 3.3% away. Its best run was 21.2R. One example, and most tries still lose small.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, no buys in the 3 days before a report)

questions.q: Two stocks both close back over their 50-day today. What's the first thing that tells a Remount from a U&R?
questions.why: Time spent under the line. A U&R dips under and is back over within a few sessions. It's a shakeout. A Remount actually lost the line, lived under it for a while, then took it back. So count the closes under the line before you name it. Volume, the 200-day's slope and an earnings gap can move the grade, but they don't change what the setup is.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line before you name it.

wrong.How heavy the volume was: Volume can raise the grade. It doesn't decide which setup you have.
wrong.Whether earnings gapped it: A remount on an earnings gap is still a Remount. The gap doesn't name it.
wrong.Whether the 200-day is rising: That's a grade cue. It doesn't split a U&R from a Remount.

questions.simple: Count the days under the line. A quick dip and back is a U&R, a real stay under is a Remount.

reasons: +2 the border between the two setups is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Move the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first ___ by default.
questions.why: Trim. The stop goes to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: First trim, stop to breakeven.

questions.q: How far away is your stop?
questions.why: 3.2%. 86.24 minus 83.52 is 2.72 a share. 2.72 over 86.24 is 3.2%. That's just past the 3% where I like my stops, and well inside 5%, so the stop width works. The wider stop just means fewer shares, so the dollar risk stays the same. Always measure it before you size. This was PYPL in October 2018, and it stopped out the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your stop in percent before you size the trade.
questions.simple: Take the buy minus the stop, then divide by the buy. That comes to about 3.2 percent.

reasons: +2 computed key

wrong.2.7%: That's the dollar gap, 2.72, read as a percent. Divide it by the buy first.
wrong.0.3%: A decimal slip. 2.72 over 86.24 is 3.2%, not 0.3%.
wrong.96.8%: That's the stop divided by the buy. Subtract first, then divide.

questions.story: A 200-day remount, then a quiet day. You buy over its high at 86.24, and your stop goes a few cents under its low, at 83.52.

questions.q: Before tomorrow's open, where's your 3R mark?
questions.why: 120.10. One R is your risk per share: 109.42 minus 105.86 is 3.56. Three of those is 10.68. Add that to your buy and 3R sits at 120.10. Mark it on the chart so you always know where you stand. It's a mark, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment call, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It's a mark, not an order.
questions.simple: Your risk per share times three, added to your buy. That's where 3R sits.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the third at 3R is a rulebook rule

wrong.$116.54: That adds 3R to the stop. Count up from your buy.
wrong.$112.98: That's only 1R. You forgot to times it by three.
wrong.$98.74: That's 3R under your buy. You subtracted.

questions.story: The quiet day after a 50-day remount. You buy over its high at 109.42, with your stop at 105.86.

questions.q: A close back under the line after the buy is an extra exit before the stop.
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit. A close back under the line is not an extra exit; the trade is held while it stays above the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. A close under the line is a warning only.

questions.q: You're in a Remount, and your stop goes a few cents under the quiet day's low. How do you place it?
choices: A real order with the broker
In your head, you'll watch it
Only on a close under the low
questions.answer: A real order with the broker
questions.why: A real order with the broker. Every position gets one, a few cents under the low, not right on it. A stop in your head fails exactly when you need it, on the day it drops fast and you hesitate. A close-only stop lets a bad day run much further than you planned. Place it when you buy. After that it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Real order, a few cents under the low, placed when you buy.

wrong.In your head, you'll watch it: A mental stop is the one you talk yourself out of. It has to be a real order.
wrong.Only on a close under the low: That lets a drop during the day run past your risk. The stop is a live order.
wrong.None until it's up 1R: The stop comes first, before the size. No trade goes on without one.

questions.simple: Put a real stop order in with your broker when you buy. A stop in your head doesn't count.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, F62)
which low anchors the stop is held (D-008)

questions.q: A Remount mostly fails by gapping straight through your stop.
questions.why: False. It mostly fails by going nowhere. Price chops back and forth around the line, the trade just sits, and your money's stuck in it. That's why we have the time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, you sell it. A gap through the stop can happen in any trade. It's not this setup's main problem.
questions.lesson_line: Remounts die in the chop. The time stop gets your money back.
questions.simple: False. The main way it fails is chop around the line, and the time stop gets you out of that.

deeper.trap: StockCharts makes the same point about moving average crosses: in sideways markets they're less reliable. A line the stock keeps crossing gives you whipsaw, not a trend.

questions.q: It's taken the line back. What are you waiting for before you buy?
choices: A quiet inside day above it
A red day on heavy volume
A wide green day on big volume
A close back under the line
questions.answer: A quiet inside day above it
questions.why: A quiet inside day above it. The retake is step one. Then I want one calm day that holds over the line, inside the remount day's range. That's the stock showing you the line is holding. Its high is your trigger: buy with a market order as price trades through it. Its low is your stop, a few cents under. NKE did exactly that in August 2020, with a stop just 1.2% away.
questions.lesson_line: Retake, quiet day, then buy the break of its high.

wrong.A red day on heavy volume: That's selling, not a pause. You want a quiet day that holds the line.
wrong.A wide green day on big volume: That's a chase day, not a quiet one, and your stop would be way too wide.
wrong.A close back under the line: That kills it. A close back under before the trigger means no trade.

questions.simple: Wait for a calm inside day that holds above the line. Buy over its high, stop under its low.

reasons: the pause entry is card 13's proposed Entry B, held (D-003)

questions.story: After a short dip under the 50-day, the stock closes back over it today on a strong green candle.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On a normal day, the stop only moves ___.
questions.why: Up. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule. On a gap-down day, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: Up, never wider.
questions.simple: The stop only moves up, never down or wider, apart from the one gap rule.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: A $9 stock that trades $30 million a day clears our liquidity floors.
questions.why: False. There are two floors and you need both: $10 a share and $20 million a day. The $30 million clears the dollar volume easily. The $9 price fails. However liquid it looks, we don't trade it under $10.
questions.lesson_line: $10 a share and $20 million a day. You need both.
questions.simple: False. It trades enough, but the price is under our $10 floor.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A pullback or U&R; line not lost
An Oops; it was a one-session dip
A new base; the 50-day is lost
questions.answer: A pullback or U&R; line not lost
questions.why: A pullback or a U&R. The stock closed under the 50-day for only two sessions, so the line was never really lost. A Remount needs the line lost for real first. The strong candle back does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A two-day dip is not a lost line.

wrong.A Remount; the 50-day was retaken: It retook the line, but the line was never really lost. Two closes under is a dip.
wrong.An Oops; it was a one-session dip: An Oops is one session that opens under the prior close. This took two closes under.
wrong.A new base; the 50-day is lost: A base is a long stay under the line, not a two-session dip.

questions.story: A leader closes under its 50-day for two sessions. Then it closes back above with a strong candle.
questions.simple: It is a pullback or a U&R, because two closes under the 50-day is a dip and not a lost line.

reasons: +2 what counts as a lost line is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.why: The AVWAP reclaim. A line that starts at one event day and bends with volume is the AVWAP. A Remount's line is a moving average or a flat price level that held before it broke. The 50-day and 200-day do not start at an event day, and a flat level does not bend.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line. A bending line from an event day is not a Remount.

wrong.A 50-day Remount: A Remount uses the 50-day or the 200-day, which do not start at one event day.
wrong.A flat-level Remount: A level Remount uses a flat price level that held. This line bends with volume.
wrong.An Oops, one session: An Oops is one session that opens under the prior close. It has no line like this.

questions.story: A stock closes over a line that starts at its August high and bends with volume.
questions.simple: It is the AVWAP reclaim, because the line starts at one event day and bends with volume, which a Remount line does not.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (k20)

questions.q: It then holds the 50-day for weeks and tops at 61.47. How many R is that from your 59.54 buy?
questions.why: 1.75R. Your risk was 59.54 minus 58.44, so 1.10 a share. The best it did was 61.47, which is 1.93 over your buy. 1.93 over 1.10 is 1.75R. So you took the planned loss and missed a move that never reached 3R anyway. The level was right. The trigger just didn't run. That was DOCU in March 2024, and it's a normal cost of trading this setup.
questions.lesson_line: The level was right and the trigger didn't run. That happens.
questions.simple: The gain per share divided by the risk per share. That's 1.75R, still short of 3R.

deeper.example: DOCU, March 2024: bought at 59.54, and it fell through the stop right away. The stock then held its 50-day for 20 sessions and traded up to 61.47. It never reached 3R. The stop did its job.

reasons: +2 computed key

wrong.2.75R: That measures from your stop, not from your buy.
wrong.1.93R: That's the dollar gain per share, 1.93. Divide it by the 1.10 risk to get R.
wrong.0.03R: That divides the gain by the price. R divides by your risk per share.

questions.story: You bought a 50-day remount over the quiet day's high at 59.54, stop at 58.44. It falls straight through your stop and you're out.

questions.q: That stop's wider than you like. What do you do?
choices: Wait for a tighter entry or pass
Tighten the stop so full size fits
Full size, accept the extra risk
questions.answer: Wait for a tighter entry or pass
questions.why: Wait for a tighter entry, or pass. I want my stops at 1-3%, and up to 5% I'll accept. At 5.5% you're past that. Sure, fewer shares would keep the dollar risk the same. But a stop that wide means a small position, so even a winner barely moves your account. A tighter trigger lets you carry real size for the same risk. And never pull the stop up to fit more shares. Normal noise takes you right out.
questions.lesson_line: Past 5%, I wait for a tighter spot. I never squeeze the stop to fit.

wrong.Tighten the stop so full size fits: Then the stop isn't where the chart says you're wrong, and noise takes you out.
wrong.Full size, accept the extra risk: The size comes from the stop. Full size on a 5.5% stop blows way past your risk.
wrong.Use a close-only stop instead: That isn't a real order, and it lets the loss run even further.

questions.story: A clean Remount sets up. The quiet day's low is 5.5% under where you'd buy, and that's where the honest stop goes.
questions.simple: It's past the 5 percent we accept. Wait for a tighter entry or pass, and never squeeze the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13)

questions.q: The gap went through your stop. What's the play?
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes decide, and that bar's low becomes your new stop. But there's a ceiling. If those 30 minutes take you past 2R, you're out. 2R under 47.20 is 44.80, and the low hit 44.40. That's past it. The gap rule gives a stock a little room after an ugly open. It never lets one trade turn into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Hold, 44.40 is the new stop: It would be, except it's past the 2R ceiling at 44.80. Past 2R you get out.
wrong.Hold, 46.00 is still the stop: Price is already under it. On a gap, the first 30 minutes set the new stop.
wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper: That's adding to a loser, and this one just gapped through your stop.

questions.story: You bought at 47.20 with the stop at 46.00, so 1R is 1.20 and 2R under your buy is 44.80. Next morning it gaps down to 45.50. The first 30-minute bar's low is 44.40.
questions.simple: The first 30-minute low is past 2R under your buy, so you get out.

deeper.counter: Had that first 30-minute low held above 44.80, it would be your new stop and you'd stay in. The ceiling only bites when the open is this ugly.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
the key is a comparison against 2R

questions.q: It gapped right past your 3R. What do you do at the open?
choices: Your call, selling some is fine
Sell the whole thing at the open
questions.answer: Your call, selling some is fine
questions.why: It's your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. That said, three days up and a gap on top is a push. Selling some into strength like that is often smart. Holding it all and trailing is fine too. Just don't sit there waiting for 104.82 to come back. If it's really running, you may never see it again.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R is a choice, not an order.

wrong.It's an automatic sell at 3R: We don't have one. Selling part on a big gap is judgment, never a rule.
wrong.Wait for a pullback to 104.82: You may never see it. If you want to sell, sell into the strength.
wrong.Sell the whole thing at the open: That cuts your runner. The few that keep going pay for the losers.

questions.story: You bought at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98, so your 3R is 104.82. It pushes up three days in a row, then opens at 106.00.
questions.simple: A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling some into the push is your call, and so is holding.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 140 shares. 0.5% of 100,000 is $500 at risk. 109.42 minus 105.86 is 3.56 a share. 500 over 3.56 is 140.4, so round down to 140. Always round down, so a full stop-out costs the $500 you planned and not a cent more. 140 shares is nowhere near the 40% position cap, so the stop sets the size. That 3.3% stop is a bit wide for me, and the smaller share count is what pays for it.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Round down, every time.
questions.simple: Risk 500 dollars, divide by 3.56 a share, and round down. That's 140 shares.

deeper.trap: Don't round up. One extra share pushes a full stop-out past the $500 you chose to risk. Rounding down keeps the loss inside the plan.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the sizing rule is in the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

wrong.141 shares: You rounded up. One more share and a full stop-out costs more than $500.
wrong.365 shares: That's sizing to the 40% cap. The stop allows far fewer.
wrong.1,404 shares: You moved the decimal and risked ten times what you meant to.

questions.story: A 50-day remount. You buy over the quiet day's high at 109.42, stop at 105.86. Your account is 100,000 and you're risking 0.5% on this one.

questions.q: What do you trail the rest with?
choices: The 9 or 20 EMA, by how it moves
A 3-day line, to keep it tight
questions.answer: The 9 or 20 EMA, by how it moves
questions.why: The 9 or 20 EMA, depending on how it trades. A fast mover gets the 9 EMA. A steadier one gets the 20 EMA, so a normal shakeout doesn't knock you out. Either way, you sell what's left on a close below it. The 200-day you just retook is way too slow. You'd hand back most of the move before it ever broke.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier name, 20 EMA. Sell the close below.

wrong.The 200-day you just took back: Far too slow. You'd give back most of the move first.
wrong.The 50-day, on every Remount: Our trail lines are the 9 and 20 EMA. The 50-day gives back too much.
wrong.A 3-day line, to keep it tight: Way too tight. Normal noise shakes you out of a runner.

questions.simple: Trail the rest under the 9 EMA if it's fast, the 20 EMA if it's steadier. Sell on a close below.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, adjustable)

questions.story: A 200-day remount bought over the quiet day's high at 86.71, stop at 84.91. You've sold some into a push, and the rest is still running.

questions.q: It's just sitting there. What do you do?
questions.why: Sell it and free the money. Still under 1R after 10 trading days, it goes. Chop is how this setup fails, and a trade that's gone nowhere for two weeks is chopping. The stop hasn't hit, but that money could be in something that's working. If it sets up again later, you can buy it again as a new trade with its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days, under 1R, it's out. Dead money goes back to work.

wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't hit: The stop isn't the only exit. The time stop is one too.
wrong.Add while the stop holds: Adding isn't the plan, least of all to dead money. One price, one stop.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: That move comes somewhere from 2R to 5R. At 0.5R it isn't earned.

questions.story: Ten trading days after your buy, the stock sits at 0.5R. The stop hasn't been hit and you haven't sold any.
questions.simple: Under 1R after 10 trading days, you sell it. That money should be in something that's working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: It's working fast. When do you think about your first sell?
choices: Day 3 or later, into a push
Never, hold it all for the trail
questions.answer: Day 3 or later, into a push
questions.why: Day 3 or later, into a push. We very rarely sell on day 1, and a stock up 3R in two sessions is your best trade going. Cutting it now caps it. I want to sell some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or up around 5 to 10R. There's no fixed third at 3R. It's a judgment call each time. Sell some into strength and trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely day 1. Day 3 or later, into a push.

wrong.Day 1, the second it's green: We very rarely sell on day 1. That cuts the trades that work best.
wrong.A third at exactly 3R, always: No fixed rule. The first sell is judgment, often into a push.
wrong.Never, hold it all for the trail: We do sell into strength. The trail is for what's left.

questions.simple: Rarely on day 1. Wait until day 3 or later and sell some into a push.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, adjustable)

questions.story: You bought over the quiet day's high at 20.95, stop at 20.55. Two sessions later it's already up 3R.

questions.q: Most Remount tries end as small wins.
questions.why: False. Most tries lose, and they lose small. The line gets taken back, lost again, and the stop takes it within days. The few that run pay for all of those. So the real mistake is cutting a runner early to lock in a quick gain. Do that and you keep every loser and throw away what pays for them.
questions.lesson_line: Most lose small. The runners pay for the rest.
questions.simple: False. Most tries lose small, and the few big runners pay for them, so don't cut those early.

deeper.trap: In the replay behind this setup, about 4 in 5 trades hit the first stop within 60 sessions. A win rate like that only works when the winners are big. Judge it by what the runners pay, not by how often it wins.

reasons: the deeper note cites the replay's 4-in-5 figure, which changes with the data

questions.q: What's the plan from here?
choices: Sell it all, a win is a win
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.why: Hold, and sell more into pushes. You've already sold some and your stop's at breakeven. Short of a gap, the worst case on the rest is a scratch. This one's the trade that pays for the losers. Most Remounts lose small, so when one runs, let it. Sell more into the next 3, 5 or 7 day push. Trail the rest on the 20 EMA, and a close below it sells the last piece.
questions.lesson_line: Let the runner run. Sell into pushes, trail the rest.

wrong.Sell it all, a win is a win: That's the kind of trade that pays for all the small losses. Don't cut it.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Add more, it's working: Not the plan. Adding to a winner is rare, a feel call. Here you sell into pushes.

questions.story: You sold some into a push and moved the stop to breakeven. The stock sits at 4R, above its 20 EMA, and you're itching to cash out.
questions.simple: Hold it. Sell more into strength and let the trail sell the rest, since this one pays for the losers.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52)
the replay figure comes from a dated run

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Only on a new trigger, as a new trade
Yes, it is the same setup
questions.answer: Only on a new trigger, as a new trade
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, at most 3 a week and 6 a month on one stock.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a signal. Wait for a new trigger.

wrong.Yes, it is the same setup: The same setup is not a trigger. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: A wider stop to get back in is the mistake, not the fix.
wrong.Yes, at double size: Doubling to win it back makes a small loss bigger.

questions.story: Your first Remount stopped out. Four sessions later the stock closes back over the 200-day again.

questions.q: Remounts work best while the index is still under its own 200-day.
questions.why: False. They work best coming out of a correction. That's when the indexes take back their lines and the leaders go first. With the index still under its 200-day, a Remount is weaker. The market isn't behind it, so the stock's fighting the tide. You can still take one, just expect less from it.
questions.lesson_line: The best Remounts come as the market turns up.
questions.simple: False. They're best as the market comes out of a correction, and weaker with the index under its 200-day.

deeper.trap: Weak is a read, not a ban. With the index under its 200-day, the trigger, the stop and the size work the same way. The 200-day rule for the stock itself never bends.

reasons: the index-under-its-200-day line is proposed on card 32 and held (D-023)

questions.q: The app's market filter reads Red. A clean Remount triggers on a leader today. Letting it go is the right call.
questions.why: True. Red on our market filter means mostly cash. It's a guide, not a hard rule. But in Red the market's working against every long you take. A Remount needs buyers to show up and hold the line. Let this one go. The best ones come after a correction, when the leaders take their lines back first.
questions.lesson_line: Red is mostly cash. Good setups can wait.
questions.simple: True. Red means mostly cash, so even a clean setup can wait for a better market.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)

questions.q: Strong close back over the line. Do you take it?
questions.why: Pass. That's a chop line. When price has sawed back and forth across a flat average for weeks, nobody's defending it. A close over it proves nothing. This was MSFT in November 2024. It had flipped sides of its 200-day over and over, and the try stopped out at 0R. We want a line that held, then broke. Not one the stock walks through every week.
questions.lesson_line: A line it crosses every week isn't a line. Pass.

wrong.Pass, the candle is weak: The candle's fine. The line is the problem.
wrong.Take it, it closed above: It's closed above this line plenty of times. That's exactly the problem.
wrong.Take it at half size: Half size on a chop line is still a chop trade.

questions.story: The stock closes back over a flat 200-day on a strong green candle. Over the past weeks it has crossed back and forth over that same line again and again.
questions.simple: Pass. A flat line the stock keeps crossing isn't a level anyone defends, so taking it back means little.

reasons: the chop count is held (D-075) and is never keyed

deeper.counter: StockCharts says crossover signals are less reliable in sideways markets. Weinstein's stage work says to avoid trading the sideways chop, since there's no defined trend.

questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The one that clears every average
Both grade the same; each is a pass
The one with the tighter stop
questions.answer: The one that clears every average
questions.why: The one that clears every average. Clearing all the averages at once is an A plus cue. Leaving the 50-day overhead and falling is a B minus cue. These are cues, not a fixed score. The grade sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Clear every average at once. That is the A plus picture.

wrong.The one with the 50-day overhead: Leaving the 50-day overhead and falling is a B minus cue.
wrong.Both grade the same; each is a pass: Clearing every average at once is an A plus cue; a falling average overhead is not.
wrong.The one with the tighter stop: The story gives no stops. Our card's grade cues are about the averages, not the stop width.

questions.story: Two remounts of the 200-day. One also clears the 20 and 50-day at once. The other leaves the 50-day overhead and falling.
questions.simple: Clearing every average at once is an A plus cue, and a falling 50-day overhead is a B minus cue.

reasons: +2 grading is discretionary in the account rulebook (E50)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Light volume on the retake. What's your call?
choices: Wait for the quiet day first
Pass, it wasn't under long enough
Buy it now, on the close
questions.answer: Wait for the quiet day first
questions.why: Wait for the quiet day. Light volume doesn't kill a Remount. Volume raises the grade, it's not a must. It just doesn't earn the extra credit here. A light drift back over a line it lost on heavy volume is a softer retake. So I want the quiet day to show me the line's holding. Then you buy over its high, with the stop a few cents under its low.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume, no extra credit. Still wait for the quiet day.

wrong.Pass, light volume kills it: Volume only raises the grade. It's not a must.
wrong.Pass, it wasn't under long enough: Three weeks under is a line lost for real.
wrong.Buy it now, on the close: The close back over is the retake, not the buy. We buy over the quiet day's high.

questions.story: A stock lost its 50-day on heavy volume and stayed under it for three weeks. Today it drifts back over and closes above the line on light volume.
questions.simple: Volume only raises the grade, so light volume doesn't kill it. Wait for the quiet day and buy over its high.

deeper.counter: IBD reads a weak, low-volume rise after a heavy drop to the 50-day as a chance to sell. That's why it earns no extra credit here. We still let the quiet day decide.

reasons: the volume rule is proposed on card 13 and held (D-006)

questions.q: Three closes under, then back over. Remount or U&R?
choices: A U&R, a quick dip and back
questions.answer: A U&R, a quick dip and back
questions.why: A U&R. Three closes under the 50-day and straight back is a quick dip, a shakeout. A U&R gets back over within a few sessions, and you buy it as the level's retaken. A Remount means the line was lost for real, with the stock living under it for a while first. This one never really lost it. It can still be a trade, you're just trading a different setup.
questions.lesson_line: A quick dip and back is a U&R. A long stay under is a Remount.

wrong.An Oops, a one-day undercut: An Oops is one session. This one closed under three times.
wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: It never really lost the line. Three closes under is a dip.
wrong.A breakdown, so you sell: It's already back over the line. That's a retake, not a breakdown.

questions.story: It closes back over its 50-day today. Before this, it had closed under the line only three times.
questions.simple: Three closes under and right back is a quick dip. That's a U&R, not a Remount.

deeper.trap: Both setups end with a close back over a line, so that close won't tell you which one you have. Count the closes under the line first.

reasons: +2 the border with the Remount is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What setup did Tuesday just hand you?
choices: A Remount of a lost level
questions.why: An Oops. It all happened in one session. Tuesday opened under Monday's close, traded under Monday's low, then closed back over Monday's close. That's the whole pattern. For a Remount you need a line the stock lost for real. That's an average or a level it lived under for a while. One day can't give you that.
questions.lesson_line: One day, under the low and back over the close. That's an Oops.

wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: There's no 50-day in the story, and one day can't lose a line for real.
wrong.A Remount of a lost level: No level was lost over days. This was one session.
wrong.An AVWAP reclaim: There's no event day or anchored line here.

questions.story: Monday closes at 40.00 with a low of 39.50. Tuesday opens at 39.20, trades down to 39.00, then rips and closes at 40.30.
questions.simple: Open under the close, trade under the low, close back over. All in one day is an Oops.

deeper.trap: An Oops and a Remount both end with a close back over something, so check what. An Oops only needs the prior day's low and close. A Remount needs a line you can see it really lost.

reasons: +2 the border with the Remount is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: There's no average in play here. What are you looking at?
choices: A Remount of a price level
questions.answer: A Remount of a price level
questions.why: A Remount, the level kind. 100.00 was a real floor. It held for months, and everyone who bought the breakout knows that number. Then it broke and the stock lived under it for three weeks, so it was lost for real. Now it's back. You trade it just like an average Remount. Wait for the quiet day, buy over its high, stop a few cents under its low.
questions.lesson_line: A level that held, broke and got taken back. Same trade.

wrong.An AVWAP reclaim: An AVWAP starts at one event day and bends with volume. This one's a flat price.
wrong.A 50-day or 200-day Remount: The line here is a price, 100.00, not an average.
wrong.A U&R of the 100.00 level: A U&R is back over within a few sessions. This sat under for three weeks.

questions.story: A stock broke out over 100.00 and held above it for months. Then it closed under 100.00 and stayed there three weeks. Today it closes back over.
questions.simple: A flat price that held as a floor, broke, then got taken back. That's a Remount of a level.

deeper.counter: Not every flat price is a level. It has to have held first. A price the stock chopped back and forth through for weeks isn't a level, and buying its retake is a mistake.

reasons: the lines that count and the time under the line are held (D-073, D-074)

questions.q: Is that a Remount yet?
choices: Not yet, that's just a poke
A U&R, a quick snap back
questions.answer: Not yet, that's just a poke
questions.why: Not yet. ATR is the stock's normal daily range, and 0.08 ATR is a tiny slice of it. Tomorrow's noise could put it right back under the 50-day. I want a clear close, one that leaves no doubt the line's been taken back. ESS gave you that a few sessions later. Waiting cost you nothing there, and buying the poke would have been a guess.
questions.lesson_line: A poke isn't a retake. Wait for the clear close.

wrong.An Oops, a one-day undercut: An Oops is one session. This stock lived under the line for weeks.
wrong.Yes, a clear retake: A sliver of a day's range over the line isn't clear. It's noise.
wrong.A U&R, a quick snap back: A U&R is back within a few sessions. This sat under for weeks.

questions.story: After weeks under its 50-day, the stock closes just over it today, 0.08 ATR above the line. That's a sliver of a normal day's range.
questions.simple: Not yet. A close that barely clears the line is inside the noise, so wait for a clear close.

deeper.trap: The mistake is buying the poke itself. ESS took the line back clearly a few sessions later and ran, so waiting didn't cost the move.

reasons: the remount-day margin is proposed and held (D-075)

questions.q: It slipped back under before you bought. What now?
choices: Wait for it to close over again
Buy anyway, it's just one close
Buy half size, stop at the low
questions.answer: Wait for it to close over again
questions.why: Wait for it to close over again. A close back under the line before the trigger means no trade. The retake failed, and yesterday's close above doesn't count anymore. That's not the end of the stock though. If it closes back over later, the setup's on again with a fresh quiet day and trigger. Until then there's nothing to buy, at any size.
questions.lesson_line: Back under before the buy means no trade. Not no stock.

wrong.Buy half size, stop at the low: Half size doesn't fix a failed retake.
wrong.Buy anyway, it's just one close: That one close is the retake failing. No trade.
wrong.Write it off for good: It's off until it closes over the line again, not forever.

questions.story: The stock remounted its 200-day yesterday. Today, before your trigger fires, it closes back under the line.
questions.simple: A close back under before you buy cancels it. Wait for a new close over the line.

deeper.trap: Don't hang on to yesterday's close. Once it closes back under before your trigger, the retake is off. It's back on only after a new close over the line.

questions.q: It's through the trigger but way up. Do you buy at the open?
choices: Not here, wait for a flush
Yes, and widen the stop to fit
questions.answer: Not here, wait for a flush
questions.why: Not here. We never buy more than 4% over the buy point, and 4% over 50.00 is 52.00. You'd be filling at 52.60. Your stop still sits under the quiet day's low, so chasing costs you size, not risk. Every share is further from the stop, so you get fewer of them. On a gap like this there's one more way in. Wait for a morning flush or pullback that curls back up, and buy that.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% at the open, don't chase. Let it flush and curl.

wrong.Yes, the trigger fired: It did fire, but the fill is past 4% over the buy point.
wrong.Yes, and widen the stop to fit: Widening the stop to fit a chase is two mistakes at once.
wrong.No, the trigger never fired: It opened over 50.00, so it fired. The problem is the price.

questions.story: The quiet day's high is 50.00, so 4% over it is 52.00. This morning the stock gaps up and opens at 52.60.
questions.simple: It's more than 4 percent over the buy point. Don't chase the open, wait for a flush that curls back up.

deeper.trap: The 4% check is on your fill, not on the signal. A gap is where it bites. Your stop stays under the buy point, so a late fill means more risk per share and fewer shares.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
the key needs a percent check
which buy point counts is held (D-022)
edited at the cold check

questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: No, it's too stretched to buy
Yes, plan to sell into a push
questions.answer: No, it's too stretched to buy
questions.why: No, it's too stretched. We skip a long more than 10% over its 9 EMA, and this one's 12% over. That far above its short average, a normal pullback toward the line is a big drop. It can take your stop before the trade ever works. The trigger fired, and that doesn't matter. The stretch check comes before the order.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA, I skip it.

wrong.Yes, the trigger fired: The trigger fired, and the stretch rule still says no.
wrong.Yes, plan to sell into a push: A sell plan doesn't fix a stretched entry.
wrong.Only at half size: Half size on a stretched stock is still a stretched buy.

questions.story: The quiet day held over the line. This morning it trades over that day's high, but it's now 12% over its 9 EMA.
questions.simple: No. More than 10 percent over the 9 EMA is too stretched, and a normal pullback can hit your stop.

deeper.trap: Everything else can line up and this one still says skip. The line, the quiet day and the trigger can all be perfect. Run the stretch check before you place the order, not after the fill.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
edited at the cold check

questions.q: Everything lines up except the report. What's the play?
questions.why: No buy. We don't take new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report can gap a stock right through your stop overnight, and no stop order helps you there. Let the news come out. If it remounts on the reaction day, that's allowed, because the report's already out. And you only hold a trade through a report if it's already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Report tonight, no buy. Let the news come out first.

wrong.Wait, the trigger hasn't fired: It has. Price traded over the quiet day's high. The report is why you pass.
wrong.Buy it, the trigger fired: The trigger's fine. The report window blocks the buy.
wrong.Buy half size into it: Half size is still a new buy inside the window.

questions.story: A textbook 200-day remount has had its quiet inside day. This morning it trades over that day's high. The company reports tonight.
questions.simple: No. We don't buy in the 3 days before a report, because it can gap right through your stop.

deeper.trap: Report timing cuts both ways. Tonight's report blocks the buy. Once it's out, a remount on the reaction day is fair game. AMD did that the day after its report on 2023-10-31.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: B minus. How do you size it?
choices: No trade at a B minus
questions.why: Smaller than a normal B. The grade sets the size. A and B get normal size, A+ gets sized up, B minus or lower gets sized down. Here the 50-day is still curling lower, and it's the first try after a long fall. That's why you graded it lower. It's not a ban. You take it smaller, so being wrong costs you less.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. A B minus goes on smaller.

wrong.Same as a normal B: Only A and B get normal size. A B minus goes smaller.
wrong.Bigger, it's a fresh start: Only an A+ gets sized up.
wrong.No trade at a B minus: A lower grade isn't a ban. It's a smaller size.

questions.story: A stock fell 25% over months but never closed under its 200-day. Today it takes back its 50-day for the first time, and the 50-day is still curling lower. You grade it a B minus.
questions.simple: A B minus gets sized down. You still take it, just smaller, so being wrong costs less.

deeper.trap: A weak cue lowers the grade. It doesn't ban the trade. Grading is a judgment call, so treat each cue as one input.

reasons: +2 grade and size rest on the account rulebook (D38, E50)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: It beat the index back over the line. How does that change your read?
questions.why: It raises the grade. A leader that takes its line back before the index is telling you somebody wants it. And that's while the market's still shaky. Coming out of a correction, the leaders take their lines back first, and this is what that looks like. It's one input though. You still need the close over the 200-day, the quiet day and a real stop.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders take their lines back first. That raises the grade.

wrong.It's a warning, it's early: Leaders move first. That's strength, not a warning.
wrong.Nothing, ignore the index: The index matters. Beating it back over the line is a plus.
wrong.It's an automatic A+: Grading is judgment. This is one input, not the whole grade.

questions.story: A leader lost its 50-day in a market shakeout. It takes the 50-day back while the index is still under its own 50-day, though above its 200-day.
questions.simple: A leader taking its line back before the index is strength. It raises the grade.

deeper.trap: The cue raises the grade, not the rules. It still needs the close over the 200-day, the quiet day and a real stop order.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50: grading is a judgment call)

questions.q: Where does that leave you?
choices: Nothing; wait for a fresh trigger
Buy back at 59.54; the line held
Buy now and skip the stop this time
Widen the stop on the next try
questions.answer: Nothing; wait for a fresh trigger
questions.why: Nothing. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop. It is limited to 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. DOCU gapped under its stop on 2024-03-15, then held the 50-day for the next 20 sessions and traded up to 61.47. The level was right; the trigger did not run.
questions.lesson_line: Right level, wrong trigger. Wait for a new one.

wrong.Buy back at 59.54; the line held: The line held, but the trigger is gone. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next try: The stop sits under the low it marks. Widening it only makes the loss bigger.

questions.story: You bought at 59.54 with the stop at 58.44. A gap under the stop the next morning ended it. The stock then held its 50-day for 20 sessions.
questions.simple: Do nothing now. A second try needs a fresh trigger and its own stop, even when the line held.

deeper.trap: Hindsight makes the stop look wrong, but the stop did its job. DOCU gapped under 58.44 the next morning and the trade ended there. A right level is not a right trade: the stock reached only +1.75R inside the window, short of the 3R trim.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)

questions.q: You got shaken out, then it ran without you. What's the lesson?
choices: That's the cost of the setup
questions.answer: That's the cost of the setup
questions.why: That's the cost of the setup. You bought it right and the stop did its job. The next day traded under it and took you out, and it turned around later without you. That happens. Most tries lose small, and some of those losers go on to work. You can't know which ones ahead of time. The stop is what keeps the ones that don't work small. That was FDX in 2018.
questions.lesson_line: Some stops are shakeouts. That's the price of being in the ones that work.

wrong.Widen stops on these names: The stop never goes wider. Wider stops just mean bigger losses on the ones that fail.
wrong.Skip stops on 200-day names: Every trade gets a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Buy back at 206.55 next time: A new try needs its own trigger and stop, not a price from the old trade.

questions.story: A 200-day remount bought at 198.12 with the stop at 195.31. The next day's low hits 193.94 and you're stopped. Weeks later it reaches your old 3R, 206.55.
questions.simple: A stop-out that later turns around is the normal cost of the setup. The stop still did its job.

deeper.trap: Don't judge a stop by what the stock does after it. FDX stopped out on a low of 193.94, then reached 206.55 weeks later. If it sets up again, that's a new try with its own trigger and stop.

questions.q: Stopped the very next day. What went wrong?
questions.why: The market was against it. The S&P 500 was under its own 200-day, and in a market like that even a clean Remount is a weaker bet. The stock's trying to go up while the index drags on it. Look at the chart too. AAPL's own 50-day sat under its 200-day. Another mark against it. That was AAPL in September 2022. It opened lower and ran through the stop the next morning. The stop did its job. Most tries lose small, and this was one of them.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index before you trust the chart.

wrong.Bad luck, nothing showed it: The clue was there. The S&P 500 was under its own 200-day.
wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop never goes wider. It was the exit and it worked.
wrong.The 200-day doesn't work: The line's fine. The market behind it was weak.

questions.story: A 200-day remount bought at 163.43, stop at 159.25. The S&P 500 sits under its own 200-day. The next day it opens at 159.90 and trades through your stop.
questions.simple: The index was under its own 200-day, so the remount was weak. The stop did its job.

deeper.trap: One loss doesn't prove the setup or the stop was wrong. A weak index makes a weak remount, and the stop kept the loss small.

reasons: +2 index under its own 200-day as a hard line is a held decision (D-023)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Big volume on the retake, weak market. How much does the volume help?
choices: Not enough to beat the market
It makes it an A+ setup
It means the stop matters less
questions.answer: Not enough to beat the market
questions.why: Not enough to beat the market. Volume raises the grade, and 2.98x is heavy. But with the index under its 200-day in a correction, a Remount is weak, and volume doesn't fix that. Look at the chart too. The 50-day still sits overhead, pointing down. That's one more mark against it. This was PYPL in October 2018, and it stopped out the session after the buy. I'll take heavy volume as a plus. I won't let it talk me out of checking the market.
questions.lesson_line: Volume helps. It doesn't beat a weak market.

wrong.It makes it an A+ setup: Volume raises the grade. It doesn't cancel a weak market.
wrong.It means the stop matters less: The stop always matters. It's what ended this one.
wrong.Follow-through is now likely: Not with the index under its 200-day. This one stopped out the next session.

questions.story: The earnings reaction day. The stock retakes its 200-day on heavy volume. The index is under its own 200-day in a sharp correction. You plan to buy over the next quiet day's high.
questions.simple: Heavy volume raises the grade, but it doesn't save a remount when the index is under its 200-day.

deeper.trap: The buy over the quiet day is a trigger, not a promise. Check the index against its own 200-day before you trust a remount, however loud the volume.

reasons: the key rests on one dossier example
the index line is proposed and held (D-023)
the old key said Nothing and was softened

questions.q: You get one buy. Which is it?
questions.why: The leader over every average. It clears every line, it's over the 200-day, the stop is 2% and the market's Green. That's the one I want. The 50-day retake still closes under a falling 200-day, and below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. The flat 200-day is a chop line. It's been crossed so often it doesn't mean anything.
questions.lesson_line: 200-day first, then the line, then the stop.

wrong.The 50-day retake: Its close is under a falling 200-day. We don't buy stocks down there.
wrong.The flat 200-day retake: Crossed ten times in 60 sessions, that's a chop line.
wrong.Pass on all three: The first one passes every check. That's a trade.

questions.story: Three remounts today. One: a leader clears every average, with a quiet day, a 2% stop and a Green market. Two: a 50-day retake with the close still under a falling 200-day. Three: a flat 200-day it crossed ten times in 60 sessions.
questions.simple: The leader. The second one is under the 200-day, and the third is a chop line.

deeper.counter: Check the 200-day first, and the 50-day retake fails it. The flat line may close over, but a line crossed ten times isn't a floor. Only the leader has the line, the quiet day, a tight stop and the market behind it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, A13, F65)
the A plus cue touches E50

questions.q: After a short dip under its 50-day, read the last two days on this chart. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it over the quiet day's high
Buy now, before the high breaks
questions.answer: Take it over the quiet day's high
questions.why: Take it over the quiet day's high. The remount day was a strong close over the 50-day, a full 1.3 ATR clear of it. The next day was an inside day that held above the line. That's the setup. Buy with a market order as price trades over the inside day's high, stop a few cents under its low. This was NKE in August 2020. The buy came at 101.19, stop 99.98, just 1.2% away, and 3R came the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Strong retake, quiet day over the line. That's the trade.

wrong.Pass, it closed under the 50-day: Look again. Both days closed over the 50-day.
wrong.Pass, the retake was marginal: It cleared the line by 1.3 ATR. That's a strong close.
wrong.Buy now, before the high breaks: The buy is the break of the quiet day's high, not before it.

questions.simple: Take it. A strong retake and then a quiet day that held the line, so you buy over its high.

deeper.example: NKE spent 7 days under its 50-day after the 2020 recovery. The close on 2020-08-05 was a strong retake, and the next day was an inside day. The buy came on 2020-08-07 at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98, 1.2% away. It ran to 25.0R.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the pause entry over a quiet inside day)

questions.q: It just closed back over its 50-day. Check the other averages on this chart. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the 50 is over the 200
questions.why: Pass. It's under the 200-day. The close was 274.51 and the 200-day sat at 295.88, so on the bigger picture it's still in a downtrend. The 50-day was under the 200-day too. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks, full stop. A 50-day retake only counts when the close clears the 200-day as well. This was CRM in June 2025.
questions.lesson_line: A 50-day retake under the 200-day is not a buy.

wrong.Take it, the 50 is retaken: Retaking the 50-day only counts with the close over the 200-day too.
wrong.Take it, the 50 is over the 200: Look again. The 50-day sits under the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass, the 50-day doesn't matter: The 50-day matters plenty. The 200-day is what blocks this one.

questions.simple: Pass. The close is under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks under it.

deeper.trap: A 50-day retake looks like a Remount, but the 200-day check comes first. Here 274.51 sat under 295.88, so it failed before anything else mattered.

reasons: +2 no longs below the 200-day is in the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: On a clean setup, it's fine to own 5% of the stock's average daily volume.
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, however clean it looks. Past that, you can't get out fast when you need to, and your own selling starts pushing the price against you. If the size your stop allows is bigger than 1% of the volume, you take less.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than 1% of the daily volume. You have to be able to get out.
questions.simple: False. We cap it at 1 percent of daily volume, so we can always get out.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only
+2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: You just sold your first piece into a push. Where does the stop on the rest go now?
choices: Up to 2R to lock in profit
questions.why: Up to your buy price, breakeven. We move the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. You've sold some, so now's the spot. Now the rest can't turn into a real loss on an ordinary pullback, and you can let it run without sweating it. The stop only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: First sell made, stop to breakeven.

wrong.Up to 2R to lock in profit: Too tight. Normal noise would knock you out of the runner.
wrong.Halfway from stop to buy: That's not something we do. Breakeven is the move.
wrong.Up to the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is a trail for what's left, used on a close below it.

questions.simple: Up to your buy price. Once you've sold some, the rest shouldn't turn into a loss.

deeper.counter: The breakeven move can come anywhere from 2R to 5R, so you don't have to wait for the first sell. Moving it down is never allowed.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook (B19)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven
Hold it all; the stop stays
questions.answer: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven
questions.why: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven. The hard rule is a third at 3R, and the stop moves to breakeven at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: Third off at 3R, stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell half; the stop stays: The hard rule is a third at 3R. The stop moves to breakeven at the first trim by default.
wrong.Hold it all; the stop stays: The first third comes off at 3R. Holding it all skips the plan.
wrong.Sell it all: The last third rides the trail. Another third comes off at 5R.

questions.story: You bought at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98. The stock trades to 104.82, which is 3R.

questions.q: Wyckoff wrote about shakeouts in a stock that's already started up. What's a sharp drop like that meant to do to holders?
choices: Lock them in for a rally
questions.why: Scare them into selling. Wyckoff describes a shakeout as a fast drop meant to get regular holders to sell their shares to the big operators. Once the weak hands are out, the big money owns the stock. You'll see the same trick on a moving average. Price undercuts the line, fakes out the sellers, then rallies back over. That's the idea behind a lot of the lines we buy back.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is built to make you sell. Know it when you see it.

wrong.Lock them in for a rally: A shakeout is meant to get holders out, not keep them in.
wrong.Juice volume for a breakout: The point is to make holders sell, not to make volume.
wrong.Prove the trend has turned: In Wyckoff's picture it comes after an advance has started. It doesn't prove a downtrend.

questions.simple: A shakeout is a sharp drop meant to scare holders into selling to the big players.

deeper.example: Morales and Kacher describe the same move on a moving average: the stock undercuts it, fakes out sellers and would-be short-sellers, then rallies back above it.

questions.q: Orange market, B setup. What's the play?
choices: Take it full size, like Green
questions.why: Pass. In Orange I only want my best stuff, the A+ setups. A B can work in Yellow at a smaller size, but not here. When the market's under pressure, breakouts fail more often because the market isn't backing them. So you save your risk for the cleanest setups. The reading's a guide, not a hard cap, and Orange still lets you take an A+.
questions.lesson_line: Orange is A+ only. A B can wait.

wrong.Take it full size, like Green: Full risk is for Green. Orange wants only A+.
wrong.Take it smaller, like Yellow: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange raises the bar to A+.
wrong.Pass, Orange means no trades: Orange still allows an A+. Red is mostly cash.

questions.story: The market reading in the app is Orange: under pressure, one step from Red. A Remount sets up cleanly, but you grade it a B.
questions.simple: Orange means only A+ setups. A B waits for a better market.

deeper.trap: Don't treat Orange as a smaller Yellow. Yellow cuts the size and the number of positions. Orange raises the bar to A+ only. A B you'd take smaller in Yellow just waits in Orange.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, the market reading)

questions.q: It's back under the line you bought. Do you sell?
choices: No, the stop is the exit
questions.answer: No, the stop is the exit
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit. A close back under the line after you're in isn't a second exit. You put the stop where the chart says you're wrong, at 44.80, and price is still above it. Selling on the close under the line would put two exits on one trade, and they'd fight each other. Hold it and let the stop do its job. The time stop still applies if it goes nowhere.
questions.lesson_line: Slipped under the line, still over the stop. Hold.

wrong.Yes, sell, the line failed: A close under the line isn't an exit. The stop is.
wrong.Raise the stop to 46.01: Breakeven comes somewhere from 2R to 5R. You're not there.
wrong.Add more on the dip: That's adding to a loser. One price, one stop.

questions.story: You bought a 200-day remount at 46.01 with the stop at 44.80. Three days later it closes at 45.60, back under the 200-day but above your stop.
questions.simple: No. It's still above your stop, and the stop is the exit, not a close under the line.

deeper.trap: Don't treat a close under the line as a second stop. The plan has one exit, the stop, plus the time stop for a trade stuck under 1R after 10 trading days. A close under the line is a warning to watch.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-008, what a close back under the line means after the buy)

questions.q: Which grades highest?
choices: B; leader first, all averages clear
A; it finally turned after a long fall
C; it retook the 50-day, rest overhead
They all grade about the same
questions.answer: B; leader first, all averages clear
questions.why: B. A leader that remounts before the index is an A plus cue, and so is clearing all the averages at once. A is a first attempt after a long decline and C leaves the averages overhead and falling, so both are B minus cues. These are cues, not a score.
questions.lesson_line: Leader first, every average cleared: that is the A plus picture.

wrong.A; it finally turned after a long fall: A first attempt after a long decline, or a line still curling lower, is a B minus cue.
wrong.C; it retook the 50-day, rest overhead: A retake that leaves averages overhead and falling is a B minus cue.
wrong.They all grade about the same: Grade follows the cues, and these are far apart.

questions.story: Three remounts. A: a first try after a long decline, the line still curling lower. B: a leader that remounts before the index and clears every average. C: the 50-day retaken, other averages overhead and falling.
questions.simple: B grades highest. A leader that remounts before the index and clears every average is the strongest picture, while A and C are weaker.

deeper.trap: The trap is adding up cues like a checklist. A cue is a hint about how much to like a setup, not a score. Here B shows two A plus cues, and A and C each show a B minus cue. The card lists cues. It does not hand out a grade.

reasons: grade cues sit against rulebook E50, which says grading is discretionary

questions.q: The line is 62.00. The deepest close under it was 60.50. ATR, the typical daily move, is 1.20. How many ATR under the line?
questions.why: 1.25 ATR. Take the line minus the deepest close, 62.00 minus 60.50. Divide that by the ATR, 1.20, to get 1.25 ATR. Our card proposes a close at least 0.5 ATR under the line, so this break left the line.
questions.lesson_line: Our card proposes a close at least half an ATR under the line.
questions.simple: Take the gap under the line and divide it by the ATR of 1.20, which gives 1.25 ATR.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only
+2 computed key

wrong.1.50 ATR: Gave the gap in dollars, no divide.
wrong.0.80 ATR: Flipped it: divided the ATR by the gap.

questions.q: Did it really lose the line?
choices: No, the dip was too shallow
Yes, the close back proves it
No, it has to lose the 200-day
questions.answer: No, the dip was too shallow
questions.why: No. A dip that only reaches 0.2 ATR under the line never really left it. ATR is the stock's normal daily range, and that's a small slice of it. That's noise around the line, not a loss of it, so there's nothing to take back. A real loss leaves the line clearly behind. This one was the 50-day holding, and you'd trade it as a pullback if anything.
questions.lesson_line: A dip inside the noise isn't a lost line.

wrong.Yes, any close under counts: A sliver under the line is noise. A real loss leaves the line behind.
wrong.Yes, the close back proves it: The close back is the retake. There has to be a real loss first.
wrong.No, it has to lose the 200-day: The 200-day is a different check. This is about the 50-day.

questions.story: A stock held its 50-day for months. It dipped under on a few closes, but the deepest was only 0.2 ATR under, a sliver of a normal day. Today it closes back over.
questions.simple: No. A dip that shallow is noise around the line, so it never really lost it.

deeper.trap: Don't call every close under a line a break. Look at how far under it closed. A sliver under a line that held for months is the line holding.

reasons: the 0.5 ATR depth is a threshold on our card that may change

questions.q: A price level only counts for a Remount if the stock actually held it before it broke.
questions.why: True. A level has to have been a floor first. Round numbers, old highs, base lows, old pivots. They matter because the stock held them and a lot of people watched it hold. If the stock chopped back and forth through a price for weeks, nobody's defending it, and taking it back means nothing.
questions.lesson_line: A level has to hold before it can be lost.
questions.simple: True. A level has to hold before it breaks, and a price the stock chopped through isn't one.

reasons: +3 one cited fact carries the key
+2 the 10 of 15 count is a proposed card number
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Is 80.00 a real level here?
questions.why: No, it never really held. A real level is one the stock respected before it broke. Here it closed on both sides of 80.00 over and over, so 80.00 was just a price it chopped through. Nobody was defending it, so taking it back means nothing. Round numbers can be great levels. This one just never acted like one.
questions.lesson_line: A price it chops through for weeks isn't a level.

wrong.Yes, the retake is enough: The retake comes second. It had to hold first.
wrong.Yes, round numbers count: Only if they held. This one got chopped through.
wrong.No, Remounts use averages: The level kind is real. This price just never held.

questions.story: A stock breaks under 80.00 and later closes back over it. In the weeks before the break, it closed above and below 80.00 over and over.
questions.simple: No. The stock chopped back and forth through 80.00, and a level has to hold before it counts.

reasons: the 10 of 15 closes line is a threshold on our card that may change

questions.q: Gap down, line still holding. What's the play?
choices: Buy it when it turns green
Buy the open, catch the dip
Wait for a close over the high
Skip it, the gap ends it
questions.answer: Buy it when it turns green
questions.why: Buy it when it turns green on the day. A gap down that holds the line is the stock getting tested. When it turns positive, the buyers just won that test. Buy at market right there, with your stop a few cents under that day's low. Don't buy the open. You'd be guessing the dip is over, and if it keeps falling you're stuck in it.
questions.lesson_line: Gap down, line holds: buy the turn to green.

wrong.Buy the open, catch the dip: That's guessing. Wait for it to turn green.
wrong.Wait for a close over the high: That waits a full day. The buy is the turn on the day itself.
wrong.Skip it, the gap ends it: Not while it holds the line. That's exactly the case for this buy.

questions.story: Yesterday was a clean remount day. Today it gaps down at the open but stays above the line. You haven't bought yet.
questions.simple: Wait for it to turn green on the day, then buy. Your stop goes under that day's low.

reasons: +2 the stop and market entry rest on the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: You can time a Remount entry on the hourly chart, off a higher low or a little flag.
questions.why: True. The hourly can time it. A higher low or a tight little flag over the line can give you a cleaner entry and a tighter stop. The daily still comes first, though. The close has to be over the line and over the 200-day before the hourly matters. An hourly that looks great while it's under the line is still a no.
questions.lesson_line: The daily sets it up. The hourly can time it.
questions.simple: True. The hourly can fine-tune the entry, but the daily close over the line still comes first.

deeper.trap: Hourly timing refines the entry. It doesn't replace the daily checks. Don't buy under the line because an hourly bar looks good.

reasons: +3 one card line carries the key

questions.q: You love how it's acting. Do you add?
choices: No, liking it isn't a reason
Yes, and move the stop to fit
No, sell it all, lock the gain
questions.answer: No, liking it isn't a reason
questions.why: No. Liking it more isn't a reason to buy more. The full size went on at one price with one stop, and that's the plan. Look at the chart. Two days in, it has already run, and it sits well over its 200-day now, a tad extended. Add up here and your average price climbs, so a normal pullback hurts a lot more. Adding to a winner on strength does happen, but it's rare and a feel call, never the plan. If it keeps working, you'll be selling some into strength soon.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. Liking it more isn't a trigger.

wrong.Yes, add half, same stop: That turns one buy into two. The full size went on once, and adding isn't the plan.
wrong.Yes, and move the stop to fit: Moving the stop to fit an add breaks the plan.
wrong.No, sell it all, lock the gain: That cuts a winner early. The first sell is judgment, into strength.

questions.story: A 200-day remount bought over the quiet day's high at 110.67, stop at 108.11. Two days later it's pushing higher on heavy volume, and you like it even more.
questions.simple: No. The full size went on once, at one price with one stop, and liking it more isn't a reason to add.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, the full size at one price with one stop, no adding)

questions.q: Before the open, you mark your levels. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 65.04. 59.54 minus 58.44 is 1.10, and that's 1R. Five of those is 5.50. Add it to your buy and 5R sits at 65.04. Mark it next to your 3R. It's a level to know, not a sell order. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or up around 5 to 10R, is often best. How the stock acts decides when.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R and 5R before the open. They're marks, not orders.
questions.simple: Your risk per share times five, added to your buy. That puts 5R at 65.04.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the third at 5R is a rulebook rule

wrong.$67.24: That's seven R, two too many.
wrong.$70.54: That's ten R, double what you were asked.

questions.story: A 50-day remount bought over the quiet day's high at 59.54, stop at 58.44.

questions.q: The trail line just broke on a close. What do you do with the last 100?
choices: Hold, it's still over the stop
questions.why: Sell them. The trail is how the last piece gets sold. You picked the 20 EMA, and a close below it is your signal. You already sold two pieces into strength, so you're closing out a good trade, not a failure. Holding past your own trail is how a big winner turns into a small one.
questions.lesson_line: Close under the trail, the last piece goes.

wrong.Hold, it's still over the stop: The trail is the exit for this piece now. A close below it sells it.
wrong.Sell half, keep 50: A close below the trail sells what's left. All of it.
