wrong.Give it one more day: That's hoping. The close below the line already gave you the answer.

questions.story: You bought 300 shares of a Remount. You sold 100 into one push and 100 into the next. Today the last 100 closes under the 20 EMA you're trailing.
questions.simple: Sell them. A close under your trail line is the exit for the last piece.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, adjustable)
the key is computed from the share counts

questions.q: Another trigger on the same stock. Can you take it?
choices: No, the month's six are used
No, the week's tries are used
questions.answer: No, the month's six are used
questions.why: No. Six tries a month on one stock is the cap, and you've used them. It's three a week too, but two this week leaves room there. The month is what stops you. Six stops in a row is the stock telling you it isn't acting right. Step away from it and put that money into something that's working.
questions.lesson_line: A new trigger is a new trade, but the cap still counts.

wrong.No, the week's tries are used: Two this week is under the three-a-week cap. The month is what's used up.
wrong.Yes, every trigger is new: Each trigger is a new trade, but every try still counts toward the cap.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: A wider stop doesn't lift the cap, and the stop never goes wider anyway.

questions.story: This month you've taken six Remount tries on one stock, two of them this week. All six hit the stop. Today it triggers again.
questions.simple: No. We take at most six tries a month on one stock, and you've used all six.

deeper.trap: Each trigger is its own trade with its own stop, and that's the trap. Every try on that stock still counts toward 3 a week and 6 a month. A wider stop is never the way back in.

reasons: +2 the try cap rests on the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: After a stop-out, a second Remount try is a new trade with its own trigger and its own stop.
questions.why: True. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, at most 3 a week and 6 a month on one stock. It is not a rescue of the first trade.
questions.lesson_line: A second try is a new trade, not a rescue.
questions.simple: True. After a stop-out you may try again only on a new trigger, and the try is a fresh trade with its own stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21 and E56)

questions.q: Which one's the stronger picture?
questions.why: The 50-day plus 100.00. When an average and a real level sit together, more people are watching that spot. The ones who trade the 50-day and the ones who remember 100.00 are all looking at the same place. Taking both back at once is the stronger picture. It's a cue toward a better grade, not a score. And the level still has to be real, one that held before it broke.
questions.lesson_line: An average and a level together. That's a spot people care about.

wrong.The 50-day alone, it's cleaner: Two lines taken back at once is stronger, not messier.
wrong.Same thing, it adds nothing: A level that held for months puts more eyes on the same spot.
wrong.The 50-day alone, levels are noise: A round number that held is a level a lot of people watch.

questions.story: Two remounts close back over their line today, everything else equal. One takes back only its 50-day. The other takes back its 50-day and the round 100.00 level together, a level that held for months.
questions.simple: The one taking back the 50-day and 100.00 together. Two lines people watch beat one.

deeper.trap: Don't just count lines. Ask if they're real. A round number the stock chopped through for weeks adds nothing, however round it is.

reasons: grade cues sit against rulebook E50, which says grading is discretionary

questions.q: The report's 8 sessions out. Can you buy it?
choices: Yes, the ban is the last 3 days
No, wait until after the report
Yes, and plan to hold through it
questions.answer: Yes, the ban is the last 3 days
questions.why: Yes. Our report ban covers the 3 days before a report, and you're 8 sessions out. Just have a plan for the report itself. You only hold through it if the trade's up 5R by then. If it isn't, you sell before the report comes out.
questions.lesson_line: 8 sessions out is fine. Plan your exit before the report.

wrong.No, wait until after the report: The ban is the last 3 days. You're well outside it.
wrong.Yes, and plan to hold through it: You only hold through a report if you're up 5R.

questions.story: A clean remount triggers today. The company reports in 8 sessions.
questions.simple: Yes. Only the 3 days before a report are off limits, so plan to sell before it unless you're up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, no buys in the 3 days before a report)

questions.q: Someone in chat says 'that's a U&R, not a Remount.' What did the stock do?
choices: Dipped under a level, came right back
Sat under a line for weeks, then back
Gapped up over a line on big volume
Bounced off a line it never broke
questions.answer: Dipped under a level, came right back
questions.why: It dipped under a level and came right back. That's the Undercut and Rally. It undercuts the level, fakes out the sellers and the shorts, then rallies back over it fast. You buy it as the level's taken back. A Remount is the slow version: the line was lost for real, and the stock lived under it for a while first.
questions.lesson_line: Under and right back is a U&R. Under for a while is a Remount.

wrong.Sat under a line for weeks, then back: That's a Remount. A U&R comes back within a few sessions.
wrong.Gapped up over a line on big volume: A U&R dips under the level first, then comes back.
wrong.Bounced off a line it never broke: That's a pullback. A U&R has to undercut the level first.

questions.simple: A U&R dips under a level and takes it right back, fast. A Remount sat under the line first.

reasons: +2 the U&R card names the quick return, a proposed number
+1 new question

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy more than ___ above the buy point.
questions.simple: We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, because chasing cuts the number of shares.
questions.why: 4%. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: No more than 4% over the buy point.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
added so q46 applies a rule taught first

questions.q: A perfect-looking Remount that's 15% over its 9 EMA is still a buy.
questions.simple: False. More than 10 percent over the 9 EMA is too stretched, however clean the chart.
questions.why: False. We skip a long more than 10% over its 9 EMA, and 15% is way past that. A perfect chart doesn't change the math. That far over the short average, a normal pullback is a big drop. It can take your stop before the trade ever works. Let it come back toward the 9 EMA and set up again.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart doesn't excuse a stretched stock.

questions.q: Your stock gaps down through your stop at the open. What sets your new stop?
choices: The open of the gap day
questions.simple: The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. Past 2R, you get out.
questions.why: The first 30-minute bar's low. You give it 30 minutes, and that bar's low becomes your stop. That keeps you from dumping it on the first panicked print of an ugly open. There's a ceiling, though. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you just get out.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

wrong.The first 5-minute low: Too fast. Our rule gives it the first 30 minutes.
wrong.The first hour's low: Too long. It's the first 30-minute bar.
wrong.The open of the gap day: The open isn't the stop. The first 30-minute low is.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.story: The remount day. A leader over a rising 200-day lost its 50-day, then takes it back today on a clear green close. That close also clears its 20 EMA.
questions.q: No average left overhead now. What does that do for the grade?
choices: Pass until it retests the 20 EMA

wrong.Lowers it, it's stretched now: Clearing the averages isn't stretched. Stretched is more than 10% over the 9 EMA.
wrong.Nothing, only the 50-day counts: The 20 EMA and the 200-day count too, and none of them sit overhead.
wrong.Pass until it retests the 20 EMA: No retest needed. Clearing it on the close is the good part.

questions.why: It raises it. When one green close takes back every average at once, there's nothing left overhead. No line above it for stuck holders to sell into. That's the kind of remount I like most. It's a cue, not a score, and the grade is still your judgment. It still needs the quiet day and a real stop.
questions.lesson_line: Nothing overhead after the retake. That's the one I like.
questions.simple: It raises the grade. With no average overhead, there's no line left for sellers to lean on.

reasons: +2 a proposed grade cue on card 32, not an owner ruling
+1 grade cues sit against rulebook E50 (grading is discretionary)

questions.story: The market has a sharp shakeout and the index drops under its own 50-day. A leader loses its 50-day in the same drop but holds above its 200-day. Later it remounts its 50-day on a clear green close, while the index is still under its own.
questions.q: How does our card read the timing of this remount?
choices: An A plus cue: it moved first
A pass: wait for the index to remount
A B minus cue: it fought the market
No cue: the index does not matter
questions.answer: An A plus cue: it moved first

wrong.A pass: wait for the index to remount: Our card does not make a leader wait for the index. Remounting first is its A plus cue, though the market reading still applies.
wrong.A B minus cue: it fought the market: Moving back before the index is strength, not a fault. Our card lists it as an A plus cue.
wrong.No cue: the index does not matter: The index matters on our card. Its best case is after a correction, as the indexes remount their lines and leaders remount first.

questions.why: An A plus cue: it moved first. A leader that lost the line in a market shakeout, then remounted before the index, is our card's A plus cue. Our card says the setup is best after a correction, when leaders remount first. A cue is a hint, not a score.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders remount first. One that beats the index back is an A plus cue on our card.
questions.simple: Our card counts a leader that remounts its line before the index does as an A plus cue.

questions.q: Your Remount is sliding toward your stop, and you've got a feeling it'll turn. What do you do with the stop?
choices: Leave it right where it is
Lower it a bit for room
questions.answer: Leave it right where it is
questions.why: Leave it right where it is. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up. You put it where the chart says you're wrong, and you sized the trade off it. Lower it and your loss gets bigger than the size was built for. That feeling it'll turn is exactly how small losses become big ones. The one exception is a gap through the stop, where the first 30 minutes set a new one.
questions.lesson_line: The stop moves up, never down.

wrong.Lower it a bit for room: Then the loss is bigger than the size was built for.
wrong.Cancel it, watch the close: Without the order, nothing gets you out if it keeps falling.
wrong.Move it down to the 200-day: That's a much wider stop. The stop never moves down.

questions.simple: Leave it. The stop only moves up, and lowering it makes the loss bigger than you planned.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook
